paragraphs.text: This is a long essay by Gwern, written in 2020, about GPT-3, an AI program trained to predict the next word of Internet text. GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, the adjustable numbers inside it, making it 117 times larger than the earlier GPT-2. The essay asks what GPT-3's success says about how AI progress happens.

paragraphs.text: Gwern argues that GPT-3 supports the "scaling hypothesis." This is the idea that simple neural networks, programs loosely modeled on brain cells, get smarter just by being made bigger. They also need more data and more computing power. If this is true, he says, ever more intelligent systems will arrive as computing grows cheaper.

paragraphs.text: GPT-3 surprised people with meta-learning: picking up new tasks, like arithmetic or unscrambling words, from just a few examples. Its gains kept following smooth, predictable curves as it grew, with no sign yet of leveling off. Gwern explains why: to predict human writing very well, a model must learn the logic and cause-and-effect hidden in it.

paragraphs.text: Gwern admits he once doubted the scaling hypothesis, and now says he was wrong. He faults AI experts whose confident forecasts failed and who rarely admit it. Depending on investment and computing growth, he expects the 2020s to bring either a leveling off or runaway progress.

fuller.text: This long essay by Gwern, written in 2020, uses OpenAI's GPT-3 language model to argue for an idea called the scaling hypothesis. The idea is that simple neural networks, made huge and trained on huge data with huge computing power, become ever more intelligent.

fuller.text: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, the adjustable numbers inside a network, making it 117 times larger than GPT-2. It was trained only to guess the next word, yet it picks up new tasks, like arithmetic or anagrams, from a few examples. Gwern calls this meta-learning, meaning learning how to learn, and stresses that nobody built it in. Gains from size also kept following the predicted curve, with no sign of slowing.

fuller.text: The numbers come from scaling formulas in OpenAI's papers. Prediction error, in bits per character, fell from about 3.3 for GPT-2 to about 1.73 for GPT-3. Gwern projects about 1.24 with 100 to 1,000 times more computing, still short of humans at roughly 0.7. Training reportedly cost around $5 million, which he calls cheap by government or business standards.

fuller.text: Gwern offers two reasons why size might work. Predicting text first teaches letters, then words and grammar, while the last, deepest bits of error demand reasoning and understanding. A huge network holds many small sub-models, and memorizing ones lose once the data is too vast to memorize, leaving general rules.

fuller.text: Gwern admits the text-prediction argument long felt like a magic trick to him. It might have needed more text than exists, or a different design entirely. He says nobody predicted where these abilities would appear, and he does not know what bigger models will learn.

fuller.text: His conclusion is that Hans Moravec's decades-old forecasts, of human-rivaling computing arriving in the 2020s, are holding up. An appendix warns that agency, meaning goal-directed behavior, may emerge in large models even without human-made data.
